evidence.claim: From a dammed mountain lake, Bishop Creek descends toward the Owens Valley.
evidence.quote: the Middle Fork flows into Lake Sabrina.

evidence.claim: Bishop Creek descends toward the Owens Valley
evidence.quote: Bishop Creek then begins its steep descent to the Owens Valley.

evidence.claim: Route 168’s eastern segment starts at Lake Sabrina on the Sierra Nevada’s eastern slope and runs down to Bishop.
evidence.quote: The eastern segment of SR 168 has its western terminus at Lake Sabrina on the eastern slope of the Sierra Nevada. This rural mountain road runs east to the town of Bishop

evidence.claim: The drive passes Aspendell at 8,409 feet before reaching the Owens Valley town at 4,150 feet.
evidence.quote: Aspendell is an unincorporated community in Inyo County, California, United States located at 8,409 feet above sea level

evidence.claim: Caltrans designates the stretch from Camp Sabrina to Brockman Lane a scenic highway.
evidence.quote: is officially designated as a scenic highway by the California Department of Transportation from Camp Sabrina to Brockman Lane

evidence.claim: Above Aspendell, winter snow removal makes the upper road seasonal for most vehicles.
evidence.quote: The segment of the highway from Lake Sabrina east to the community of Aspendell is subject to closure to most vehicles during the winter months, usually not opening until mid- or late-April, due to snow removal.

evidence.claim: the Owens Valley town at 4,150 feet
evidence.quote: It is located near the northern end of the Owens Valley in the Mojave Desert, at an elevation of 4,150 feet (1,260 m).

evidence.claim: The state once conceived Route 168 as a highway connecting Fresno and Bishop across the Sierra.
evidence.quote: modern SR 168 was conceived as a trans-Sierra highway connecting Fresno and Bishop.

evidence.claim: The proposed High Sierra Piute Highway would have crossed 11,453-foot Piute Pass, but the two road segments were never joined.
evidence.quote: The proposed route, named the High Sierra Piute Highway, would have taken the highway over the 11,453-foot (3,491 m) Piute Pass

evidence.claim: The rugged crest and eastern escarpment would have made construction difficult, and designated wilderness areas now block the connection.
evidence.quote: The rugged Sierra crest and eastern escarpment would have made construction very difficult and today two congressionally designated wilderness areas block the way

evidence.claim: Caltrans has no plans to complete the crossing.
evidence.quote: the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) has no plans to complete SR 168 over the Sierra Nevada through wilderness areas.

evidence.claim: the two road segments were never joined
evidence.quote: However, the two segments were never connected.

evidence.claim: Starting at Lake Sabrina, the drive leads toward Aspendell, where the combined North and Middle forks of Bishop Creek flow through town.
evidence.quote: The North and Middle forks combine above and flow through the community of Aspendell

evidence.claim: Below the village, those waters enter Intake Two; the South Fork joins below that reservoir before the creek descends steeply toward the valley.
evidence.quote: below it the combined creeks are dammed at Intake Two, a reservoir. The South Fork flows into South Lake and continues through the community of South Fork (aka Habegger's) and then joins the Middle Fork below  the Intake Two reservoir. Bishop Creek then begins its steep descent to the Owens Valley.

evidence.claim: The road reaches Bishop and joins US 395.
evidence.quote: This rural mountain road runs east to the town of Bishop, then joins U.S. Route 395

evidence.claim: Lake Sabrina stores the Middle Fork of Bishop Creek behind a dam built in 1907–08.
evidence.quote: Lake Sabrina is a lake created by damming the middle fork of Bishop Creek.

evidence.claim: The dam supplied a steady flow to the power plants, making the lake part of the Bishop Creek power system.
evidence.quote: The dam was built in 1907–8 to supply a constant flow of water to the hydraulic power plants.  The lake is part of the Bishop Creek system.

evidence.claim: It took its name from Sabrina Hobbs, wife of California Nevada Power Company’s first general manager.
evidence.quote: the lake was originally named after Mrs. Sabrina (pronounced: suh-BREE-nuh) Hobbs, wife of C.M. Hobbs first General Manager of California Nevada Power Company which built the dam.

evidence.claim: Local residents say “Sah-bry-nuh,” although her name was pronounced “suh-BREE-nuh.”
evidence.quote: Local residents pronounce the lake "Sah-bry-nuh;" however, the lake was originally named after Mrs. Sabrina (pronounced: suh-BREE-nuh) Hobbs

evidence.claim: The reason for the pronunciation change is unclear.
evidence.quote: The reason for the lake's name pronunciation changing over the years is unclear.

evidence.claim: The road between Lake Sabrina and Aspendell is subject to winter closure to most vehicles, usually reopening in mid- or late April. The gate is southwest of Aspendell.
evidence.quote: The segment of the highway from Lake Sabrina east to the community of Aspendell is subject to closure to most vehicles during the winter months, usually not opening until mid- or late-April, due to snow removal. The winter road closure gate is located to the southwest of Aspendell.

evidence.claim: a dam built in 1907–08
evidence.quote: The dam was built in 1907–8

evidence.claim: Aspendell’s autumn distinction is its aspen trees, but the village itself dates to development by Gene Scherer in 1961.
evidence.quote: The town was developed in 1961 by Gene Scherer.

evidence.claim: It stands at 8,409 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: located at 8,409 feet above sea level

evidence.claim: The North and Middle forks of Bishop Creek meet above the community and flow through it, then enter the reservoir at Intake Two below.
evidence.quote: The North and Middle forks combine above and flow through the community of Aspendell and below it the combined creeks are dammed at Intake Two, a reservoir.

evidence.claim: An older settlement lies behind the area’s Cardinal Village Resort: it began as part of a mining town after gold was discovered in Bishop Creek in 1885.
evidence.quote: The seasonal Cardinal Village Resort is the only store and hotel in the area, and was originally built as a part of a mining town after gold was discovered in Bishop Creek in 1885.

evidence.claim: In fall, the community is known for its aspen trees.
evidence.quote: known in the fall for its Aspen trees

evidence.claim: Aspendell’s autumn distinction is its aspen trees
evidence.quote: known in the fall for its Aspen trees

evidence.claim: Bishop sits between the Sierra Nevada and the White Mountains, near the northern end of the Owens Valley.
evidence.quote: Bishop is immediately to the east of the Sierra Nevada, and west of the White Mountains.

evidence.claim: Its name came from Bishop Creek, named for settler Samuel Addison Bishop.
evidence.quote: The city was named after Bishop Creek, flowing out of the Sierra Nevada range; the creek was named after Samuel Addison Bishop, a settler in the Owens Valley.

evidence.claim: The Eastern Mono, also called Owens Valley Paiute, lived in settlements along rivers and snowmelt-fed springs and continue to live in and near Bishop.
evidence.quote: The Eastern Mono presently live in and near Bishop.

evidence.claim: The Bishop Paiute Tribe operates the Owens Valley Paiute Shoshone Cultural Center, displaying art and artifacts from area Paiute and Timbisha tribes and maintaining an active repatriation program.
evidence.quote: The tribe operates the Owens Valley Paiute Shoshone Cultural Center located in Bishop, California. The center displays art and artifacts from area Paiute and Timbisha tribes and has an active repatriation program through NAGPRA.

evidence.claim: near the northern end of the Owens Valley
evidence.quote: It is located near the northern end of the Owens Valley

evidence.claim: The Eastern Mono, also called Owens Valley Paiute
evidence.quote: the Eastern Mono (also called Owens Valley Paiute)

evidence.claim: lived in settlements along rivers and snowmelt-fed springs
evidence.quote: The Mono people were predominantly sedentary and settled in fixed settlements along rivers or springs which were fed by snowmelt from the eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada.

evidence.claim: Bishop Creek is also a working power system: five hydroelectric plants use its water, with some stretches carried through pipelines to increase their output.
evidence.quote: It has five hydroelectric plants owned by Southern California Edison, Bishop Creek #2–6. Bishop Creek #1 was never completed. Parts of the creek run through pipelines, or penstocks, to increase output at the power plants.

evidence.claim: Downstream, the creek’s hydroelectric system has five plants owned by Southern California Edison, numbered 2 through 6. Plant 1 was never completed.
evidence.quote: It has five hydroelectric plants owned by Southern California Edison, Bishop Creek #2–6. Bishop Creek #1 was never completed.

evidence.claim: The winter closure of Route 168 just south of the village prevents the remaining drive to Lake Sabrina and North Lake.
evidence.quote: In the winter months, California State Route 168 is closed just south of Aspendell, preventing the ability to complete the remaining drive to Lake Sabrina and North Lake by vehicle.

evidence.claim: The center’s store sells contemporary beadwork, basketry, jewelry, and quillwork alongside educational materials.
evidence.quote: Their museum store sells contemporary beadwork, basketry, jewelry, quillwork, and educational materials.
